result: The authors provide a detailed morphological description of Acanthomeridion serratum based on new specimens and CT scanning, revealing previously unknown anatomical features including ventral plates, appendages, hypostome, and ontogenetic changes in body shape.
evaluation: Claims C24-C59 collectively provide comprehensive morphological descriptions based on direct observation of specimens and CT data (Figures 3-8). The measurements, counts, and anatomical descriptions are well-documented with extensive figure references. The linear relationship between trunk dimensions (C49) is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7.

result: Acanthomeridion anacanthus is proposed as a junior subjective synonym of Acanthomeridion serratum based on morphological analysis and bivariate regression showing a linear relationship between trunk dimensions across specimens previously assigned to both species.
evaluation: Claim C33 is supported by morphological analysis and the statistical evidence in C49 (Figure 7), which demonstrates that specimens previously assigned to A. anacanthus fall within the continuous variation of A. serratum. The bivariate regression analysis provides quantitative support for this taxonomic revision.

result: The ventral plates of Acanthomeridion show morphological similarities to trilobite free cheeks, including a posterior spine comparable to genal spines and a suture path near the eye similar to opisthoparian facial sutures.
evaluation: Claims C60-C64 and C96 are supported by comparative morphological observations documented in Figures 1 and 9, with citations to established trilobite morphology (Whittington et al., 1997). The similarities in position, shape, and suture path are clearly illustrated and described.

result: Phylogenetic analyses using three different coding strategies for ventral plate homology show that when ventral plates are coded as homologous to free cheeks, Acanthomeridion is recovered sister to trilobites, but all analyses support multiple origins of cephalic sutures within Artiopoda regardless of coding strategy.
evaluation: Claims C67-C75 and C82 are supported by Bayesian phylogenetic analyses presented in Figures 10-11 and Table 1. The analyses were run with appropriate methods (MrBayes, 20 million generations, convergence checked), and results are consistent across constrained and unconstrained analyses. The treespace analysis (Figure 11) provides additional support for the distinct phylogenetic signal from different coding strategies.

result: The exopodites of Acanthomeridion differ substantially from other artiopodans, being stick-like with rows of lamellae and lacking segmentation, unlike the paddle-shaped exopodites characteristic of other members of the group.
evaluation: Claims C76-C77 are supported by morphological observations (C52-C54) and comparative analysis with citations to Schmidt et al., 2022 and Ortega-Hernández et al., 2013. The distinctive morphology is documented in Figures 3-4.

result: Features such as multipodomerous uniramous antennae and conterminant hypostomes are widespread in Artiopoda, with natant hypostomes likely having evolved repeatedly within the group.
evaluation: Claims C78-C81 are supported by citations to established literature (Zhang et al., 2007; Du et al., 2019; Zhai et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2004; Stein and Selden, 2012; Fortey, 1990; Chen et al., 2019). The inference about repeated evolution of natant hypostomes (C81) is logically derived from phylogenetic distribution.

result: Previous hypotheses about homology between eye slits/notches in petalopleurans and dorsal ecdysial sutures in trilobites have been questioned based on inferred evolutionary transitions.
evaluation: Claims C65-C66 accurately represent prior work with appropriate citations (Du et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019). These are statements about the literature rather than new findings.

result: The study employed appropriate methods including specimen collection from Chengjiang, CT scanning with specified equipment, and phylogenetic analyses using an updated character matrix with 70 taxa analyzed via Bayesian inference with three different coding strategies.
evaluation: Claims C83-C92 describe the materials and methods used in the study. These are well-documented with appropriate citations and technical details. The methods are standard for this type of paleontological and phylogenetic research.

result: The moulting strategy of breaking the exoskeleton along cephalic sutures has contributed to trilobite high diversity during the Palaeozoic.
evaluation: Claim C5 is speculative about the causal relationship between cephalic sutures and trilobite diversity. While the correlation is stated, no direct evidence is provided in this study to demonstrate that sutures causally contributed to diversity. This represents an inference rather than a tested hypothesis.

result: The path of the suture between ventral plates and cephalon passing close to the eye may represent a way to minimize damage to the eye during ecdysis.
evaluation: Claim C97 is a functional speculation about the adaptive significance of suture position. While plausible, no direct evidence is provided to test this hypothesis. This represents an inference about function based on morphology and comparison to trilobites.

result: The introduction provides background on euarthropod diversity, artiopodan morphology, trilobite suture evolution, and competing hypotheses about the origins of dorsal ecdysial sutures within Artiopoda.
evaluation: Claims C1-C23 represent background information and literature review, all supported by appropriate citations to established work. These provide context for the study but are not new findings.

result: Phylogenetic analyses recovered Petalopleurans sister to Nektaspida and Australimicola sister to Conciliterga.
evaluation: Claims C71-C72 report phylogenetic results shown in Figure 10 and supplements. These relationships were consistent across all six analyses performed.
